# Environments and Tool Interfaces {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> --- John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar writing to explain Marshall McLuhan's ideas, observed that tools reshape how people work. The line is often credited to McLuhan, but it is Culkin's, a small provenance lesson of its own. An architecture tool also shapes what a method can change and what an architect can observe. Those limits must be explicit when the method acts through the tool.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What has to sit between an AI that proposes a design change in one sentence and a tool that needs a hundred files, runs for days, and can exit cleanly without having evaluated anything?
:::

@sec-data-representations-world-models established how design state is represented to a method, and @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization introduced the search, generation, and optimization roles that act on it. However, a method's proposals are useless in a vacuum. Once a method proposes a design change (whether sizing a new cache hierarchy via Bayesian Optimization or proposing a new prefetcher via an LLM) it must actually execute that intent to gather evidence. This chapter builds the Implement stage's machinery, the execution environment.

In a traditional workflow, the architect manually builds the design, launches a simulator like gem5, a cycle-level architectural simulator, or Ramulator, a main memory simulator. The architect then parses the console output and debugs any segmentation faults or license errors. Scaling AI-driven design requires replacing human-in-the-loop debugging with direct, programmatic agent-tool interactions. However, giving an AI permission to execute a shell script is not an environment.

This chapter connects an AI's abstract intent to the stateful reality of computer architecture and Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools. We will define how to structure the read, action, and return paths, handle asynchronous execution, distinguish between tool crashes and design failures, and distill sprawling simulation logs into dense semantic observations.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Declare the read, action, and return contract in full before any candidate is measured, which is what separates an environment from a script.
- Classify a tool return so a cluster crash never down-weights an architecture candidate.
- Require every timing and power observation to carry the corner, mode, and library version it was measured under.
- Preserve the log lines a parser cannot classify so an unfamiliar warning still reaches the architect.

:::

## The Human–API Mismatch

In modern machine learning, an agent interacts with an environment such as an OpenAI Gym[^fn-openai-gym-c06] simulation through a clean, synchronous loop. It takes an action, and the environment returns a new state and a dense scalar reward.

[^fn-openai-gym-c06]: **OpenAI Gym**: The de facto standard reinforcement-learning environment API, in which an agent calls a step function with an action and receives the next state and a scalar reward. Its successor library, Gymnasium, keeps the same interface contract.

Hardware tools were built for humans, not APIs. For decades, architecture tools such as CACTI [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI], DRAMSys [@WeisEtAl2021DRAMSys], McPAT [@McPAT], or gem5 were engineered around manual workflows, assuming an architect who can read dense log files, debug build errors interactively, and interpret color-coded waveforms. Modifying a real design means navigating a disconnected stack. Inserting a custom vector block into an XR subsystem requires modifying Chisel, changing linker scripts, and hacking a Device Tree Blob (DTB). Forcing these messy realities into a standard ML environment loop without exposing their low-level details prevents the human architect from verifying physical constraints like timing and power.

This legacy breaks the familiar ML environment paradigm, creating a **semantic gap**. That gap separates the high-level semantic intent of a design ("increase the cache size to improve hit rate") from the low-level, unstructured mechanics of the tool itself. Instead of returning a simple scalar reward, EDA tools return gigabytes of unparsed logs, crash silently, or hang for days. The mismatch grows as design moves down the stack. The EDA tools at the bottom rely heavily on the tacit knowledge of physical design engineers to interpret unroutable netlists, whereas an automated method requires fully explicit, programmatic interfaces.

What makes a foundation model reliable against external software is less the transport than the discipline around it. Validated arguments, a bounded action space, and an auditable record of every call matter more than whether the call is a typed API or a shell command. Constraining generation to a typed, retrieved API surface does sharply cut the argument hallucinations that unconstrained access invites [@PatilEtAl2024Gorilla]. Tool-use research points the same way. Toolformer trains a model to invoke typed APIs for subtasks it cannot perform reliably on its own [@SchickEtAl2023Toolformer], and ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls so the model consumes each observation before choosing its next action [@YaoEtAl2023ReAct]. This maps directly to the architectural domain. While "computer use" models can visually parse GUIs and move a mouse, relying on visual GUI automation for architecture design is brittle and computationally inefficient; on real desktop tasks the strongest such agents finish only a small fraction of what a human completes [@XieEtAl2024OSWorld]. Because of this, system intent, a GUI, and simple permission to call a tool are insufficient for real architecture work. Validation, bounded action spaces, and auditable calls, rather than raw unconstrained access, keep control with the human architect, who can bound the AI's legal actions before spending cluster hours on unroutable silicon.

A second mismatch is the brownfield reality. Most AI research focuses on greenfield design, generating a brand new core or accelerator from a blank slate. In industry, however, most of an architect's job is brownfield work, as the Wilson Research Group's industry-wide verification study documents [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. This involves integrating legacy IP blocks, wrangling proprietary vendor protocols, and navigating undocumented system buses. To bridge this gap, the environment must expose structured hardware description standards. However, not all standards are equal. IP-XACT[^fn-ip-xact-c06] is a notoriously bloated XML standard; feeding raw IP-XACT to a generative model will immediately exhaust its context window with boilerplate. The environment's "Read Path" must distill heavy XML standards into lightweight JSON or YAML representations, whereas denser formats like SystemRDL[^fn-systemrdl-c06] might be read natively. This distillation allows the agent to programmatically discover and memory-map legacy AXI or TileLink[^fn-tilelink-c06] interfaces without relying on unstructured text datasheets. If an agent cannot successfully wire up a black-box memory controller to a modern coherency fabric, it cannot design a real System-on-Chip. The environment must expose interfaces for both generating new IP and integrating messy, opaque legacy components.

[^fn-ip-xact-c06]: **IP-XACT**: An IEEE standard XML schema that describes an IP block's ports, parameters, bus interfaces, and memory map so an integration tool can wire the block up automatically instead of a human transcribing a datasheet. Its completeness is exactly what makes it verbose, since one mid-sized component expands into thousands of lines of markup.

[^fn-systemrdl-c06]: **SystemRDL**: An Accellera standard for describing only a design's control and status registers, giving each field its width, access rule, and reset value, from which tools generate the matching RTL, firmware headers, and documentation. It stays compact because it describes the register map rather than the whole component.

[^fn-tilelink-c06]: **TileLink**: An open on-chip interconnect protocol used by RISC-V systems generated with Chisel, filling the role that ARM's AMBA AXI fills in commercial SoCs. Attaching a block means satisfying the protocol's handshake and cache-coherence rules, not merely connecting wires.

The stakes of that requirement are concrete. A vendor's PDF datasheet is not an interface. A timing diagram printed in one can disagree with the block's actual RTL behavior under specific burst conditions, and no automated check will notice, because nothing in the flow can read the document to compare the two. An interrogatable description turns that discrepancy into a query a tool can run, while a datasheet leaves it to be discovered after fabrication.

Recall the **Lighthouse prompt** introduced in @sec-moonshot. The prompt asks to design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XR platform. To tackle a system of this complexity, an agent relies on an overarching generator framework like Chipyard [@chipyard], which serves as the logical engine to emit the RISC-V SoC.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Why the prompt is not one function call"}
An agent working this prompt might formulate a high-level system intent to maximize spatial tracking throughput within the strict 3 W TDP thermal envelope required for an untethered XR headset. The candidate change, inserting a custom vector-capable accelerator block into the Chipyard-generated RISC-V subsystem, is not executable as one simple function call. An agent cannot merely instantiate the block; it must resolve bandwidth contention on the TileLink or AXI interconnect between the new spatial tracking accelerator and the high-bandwidth XR display controller. To handle the bursty, streaming point-cloud data from the headset's camera sensors without thrashing the core's working set, the agent might need to propose resizing the L2 cache or adding a specialized prefetcher. Furthermore, it must update the memory-mapped IO (MMIO) and Device Tree Blob (DTB) so the XR OS and drivers actually recognize the new vector block, connecting the hardware change to the software stack.
:::

A compiler must successfully emit the right memory mapping for the tensor instructions. The hardware configuration must instantiate the block. The RTL generator must pass simulation. Finally, the EDA flow must synthesize the design to check for routing congestion in the 3 nm layout. Each tool call can return exit code 0 while the Lighthouse architecture proposal itself remains unevaluated or logically broken.

Tool meaning depends on fixed context, legal actions, software and hardware specifications, tool versions, permissions, execution conditions, and explicitly defined failure behaviors. Two studies can call the exact same Ramulator binary while operating in different environments because their actions, workloads, constraints, and observation meanings differ. A computational method cannot infer these context dependencies via intuition. It requires the environment to explicitly expose what actions are permitted, what the tool returns, which states are invalid, and which runs can be repeated. Basic tool permissions are not enough, and the tools themselves compound the problem.

An AI requires fast, deterministic APIs, but hardware design relies on slow, stateful, and expensive legacy software. The environment sits between them. It gives the AI enough autonomy to explore the design space at scale while enforcing strict rules through permissions, budgets, and interface schemas. These rules ensure the agent does not propose physically impossible designs or waste compute time on broken Electronic Design Automation (EDA) runs.

## Balancing Architecture Environments

Hardware design is bound by tight time and compute constraints. Unlike software environments that can execute thousands of iterations per second, architecture tools are locked behind expensive licenses and days-long job queues. The compute required for a single physical design run is orders of magnitude slower and more expensive than a model's inference pass. As fidelity increases toward silicon, the sample budget shrinks by orders of magnitude, from millions of cheap functional checks to handfuls of expensive layout runs.

### The Multi-Fidelity Spectrum

To navigate this economic reality, we can look to the robotics community's approach of sim-to-real transfer. Rather than training a robotic arm directly in the physical world, which is slow and risks damaging hardware, researchers train the agent in a fast physics simulator and transfer the learned policy to the real robot [@OpenAI2019Rubik]. Architecture benefits from a similar pipeline by working across a multi-fidelity spectrum (@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum). The simulator is not a single tool, but a spectrum.

At the top are near-instant analytical models (spreadsheet and CACTI-class estimators) and functional ISA-level simulators that act as the "Sim", screening millions of candidates in seconds. In the middle are cycle-level C++ simulators, like gem5, that model detailed timing but abstract physics. At the bottom are RTL synthesis and VLSI physical design tools, the "Real", that enforce true physical laws like power, timing, and routing congestion.

An architecture environment must allow an agent to move systematically between these levels (@fig-simulator-tax). This requires managing significant mechanical friction. For instance, the environment must manage trace provenance: if an AI mutates a core's branch predictor, pre-recorded memory traces become structurally invalid because speculative execution paths change. The environment must be configured to determine when to regenerate functional traces versus when to safely replay them. Furthermore, the environment must abstract checkpointing and workload warm-up. An agent running full-system gem5 cannot afford to simulate Linux booting on every iteration, nor should it optimize a cache based on cold-misses during OS boot. The environment API must abstract Region of Interest (ROI) fast-forwarding so the AI is rewarded on steady-state behavior, not initialization noise. This fast-forwarding rests on established sampling methodology. SimPoint identifies a small set of representative program regions that stand in for a full run [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS derives statistical error bounds on the metrics recovered from sampled execution [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Because navigating this spectrum requires balancing conflicting physical limits, hardware specialization tightly couples the stack.

| **Fidelity Level** | **Example Tools** | **Speed** | **Physical Laws Enforced** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical | Spreadsheet, CACTI-class models | Near-instant (no execution) | None (closed-form estimates) |
| Functional / ISA | Spike, QEMU | ~30x slowdown | None (execution only) |
| Cycle-Approximate | ZSim [@ZSim], Sniper [@Sniper] | ~1,000x slowdown | Structural pipeline abstractions |
| Cycle-Level | gem5 (O3) | ~15,000x slowdown | Detailed timing, abstract physics |
| RTL Simulation | Verilator | ~30,000x slowdown | Two-state cycle logic (no timing, no X-propagation) |
| FPGA Emulation | FireSim | ~20x slowdown | Full logic, mapped to FPGA fabric |
| Physical Design | Yosys [@Yosys], OpenROAD | Hours to Days | Power, Timing, Routing, DRC |

: **Fidelity trades against speed.** An agent moves up this spectrum as design candidates mature, paying more per observation as fidelity rises, except where an FPGA buys the speed back at the cost of dedicated hardware. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[20,25,20,35]"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-simulator-tax
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The simulator tax: fidelity costs orders of magnitude, unless you burn an FPGA.** Representative slowdown of each architecture-evaluation approach relative to a roughly 3 GHz core. Software simulation slows by four to five orders of magnitude as fidelity rises toward cycle-level and RTL detail; FPGA-accelerated emulation stays within about twenty times real time, at the cost of dedicated hardware. Figures are order-of-magnitude and workload- and configuration-dependent.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal log chart of simulation slowdown versus real hardware across six approaches. Native silicon is one times. FPGA emulation (FireSim) is about twenty times slower. Functional or ISA simulation is about thirty times. Cycle-approximate simulation (ZSim, Sniper) is about one thousand times. Cycle-level simulation (gem5) is about fifteen thousand times. RTL simulation (Verilator) is about thirty thousand times slower."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Data: representative simulation throughput per fidelity rung, synthesized from
# primary sources and expressed as slowdown versus a ~3 GHz core. CPU-sim rungs
# count instructions, RTL/FPGA rungs count cycles (~comparable at IPC ~1). Anchors:
# ZSim (Sanchez & Kozyrakis 2013), gem5-class ~200 KIPS ,
# Verilator (Chipyard), FireSim. Order-of-magnitude,
# workload/config/host dependent. Accessed 2026-07-19.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter5-simulator-tax.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rungs = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter5-simulator-tax.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for d in csv.DictReader(fh):
        rungs.append({"rung": d["rung"], "example": d["example"], "slow": float(d["slowdown_vs_silicon"])})

kind = {"Native silicon": COLORS["workload"], "FPGA emulation": COLORS["evidence"]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.3))
n = len(rungs)
for i, r in enumerate(rungs):
    y = n - 1 - i
    color = kind.get(r["rung"], COLORS["methods"])
    slow = r["slow"]
    ax.hlines(y, 1, max(slow, 1.02), color=color, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter([max(slow, 1.02)], [y], s=46, color=color, edgecolor=color, zorder=3)
    tag = "1× (real time)" if slow < 1.5 else f"~{slow:,.0f}× slower"
    ax.text(max(slow, 1.02) * 1.35, y + 0.02, tag, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=color)
    ax.text(1.05, y + 0.34, r["rung"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"])
    ax.text(1.05, y - 0.30, r["example"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"])
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1, 6e5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.2)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("Slowdown versus real hardware (log)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([1, 1e1, 1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5])
ax.set_xticklabels(["1×", "10×", "100×", "1,000×", "10,000×", "100,000×"], fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.985, top=0.97, bottom=0.14)
plt.show()
```

The tiers are orders of magnitude apart. A cycle-level or RTL run is ten thousand to thirty thousand times slower than the silicon it models, so an agent that optimizes for high-fidelity evidence can afford only a handful of samples; FPGA emulation buys the speed back only by committing dedicated hardware. That order-of-magnitude cost turns moving up a tier into a design decision in its own right.

A cycle-level simulator is a trend instrument, not a meter, which is why the gem5 maintainers avoid the phrase cycle-accurate. A validation study that tuned gem5 to match a real ARM development board reported mean absolute runtime errors of 13 percent on SPEC CPU2006 and 16 to 17 percent on PARSEC, with most microarchitectural statistics landing within 20 percent [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError]. That is the residue left after the matching work rather than the error a team inherits by default. The same simulator's untuned x86 out-of-order model missed by 136 percent on average, and only configuration calibration and changes to the simulator itself brought it under 6 percent [@AkramSawalha2019Gem5X86]. An error bar therefore describes a simulator-and-target pair rather than a simulator, so a tier that reports one without naming the hardware it was validated against has reported nothing a rejection check can use. The number a tier returns is trustworthy for ranking two candidates under the same configuration, not for predicting what either will do in silicon. An environment that reports instructions per cycle (IPC) without recording that distinction invites the agent to chase differences smaller than the instrument's own error.

We are not the first to wrap architecture simulators in a standard reinforcement-learning environment. ArchGym exposes a family of simulators through a single Gymnasium-style interface and evaluates search methods against them under a fixed sampling budget [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. Its central finding sharpens the economics of the spectrum. Which search algorithm ranks best is not a fixed property of the algorithm; it depends on how many samples the budget allows, so a method that wins at a cheap fidelity tier can lose at an expensive one. We build on that precedent and push past the point where the clean Gym abstraction stops holding. Real architecture tools carry cross-call state, sit behind licenses and job queues, and span the whole multi-fidelity spectrum, and an environment that hides those realities behind `env.step()` misrepresents the cost of the evidence it returns.

The other thing the clean abstraction hides is coupling. Hardware specialization tightly couples the stack. Optimizing one parameter (like dataflow) cascades into breaking constraints across siloed simulation tools (thermal, synthesis, compilation). This coupled constraint problem is not unique to architecture. In aerospace engineering, designing an aircraft requires balancing aerodynamics, structures, and acoustics [@Sobieski1998BLISS]. Instead of building a single monolithic simulator, aerospace multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO) orchestrates fast *surrogate models* for broad exploration, reserving expensive physics simulators for final verification. AI in computer architecture should similarly orchestrate existing tools rather than replace them.

AI should act as an architectural control plane[^fn-control-plane-c06]. Rather than just generating scripts, it must take declarative intent, measure actual state from simulators and EDA tools, and issue compensating actions, such as shrinking a cache to fix a thermal violation. ChatEDA demonstrates one realization of this pattern, decomposing a natural-language design intent into subtasks that an autonomous agent then drives through a real EDA toolchain from RTL to GDSII [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA].

[^fn-control-plane-c06]: **Control plane**: In networking and cloud systems, the layer that decides what the system should do and issues the commands, held separate from the data plane that actually moves the traffic or runs the work. Casting an AI as the architectural control plane means it sets and revises intent while the simulators and EDA tools stay the machinery that executes it.

### The Silicon ADMET Funnel

This is a constraint inversion. Historically, architecture flowed top-down from intent to RTL and RTL to physical design. Today, physical limitations like thermal envelopes, wire delay, and routing congestion constrain architectural choices bottom-up.

Like drug discovery, finding a high-performance design is often easier than passing these inverted physical limits, what we might call silicon ADMET, borrowing the drug-discovery ADMET screen[^fn-admet-c06] that filters candidate compounds on downstream physical viability rather than potency alone. The multi-fidelity spectrum screens candidates by evaluation cost; the same filtering recurs along the physical axis, where data movement, thermal limits, and routing progressively reject high-scoring candidates that cannot survive signoff (@fig-silicon-admet-funnel). Architecture also faces a sim-to-silicon gap, so the AI must optimize for designs that survive physical variation and tool noise rather than fragile peaks in a proxy score.

[^fn-admet-c06]: **ADMET**: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity, the five downstream viability properties a drug candidate must clear regardless of how potent it is.

![**The "Silicon ADMET" funnel.** Drawing a parallel between the phased, rigorous filtering of drug discovery and the physical signoff funnel in computer architecture, both disciplines must weed out high-scoring "decoys" early using increasingly expensive and faithful evaluations.](images/F5-silicon-admet-funnel){#fig-silicon-admet-funnel fig-alt="Two parallel three-stage funnels. Drug discovery narrows from in-silico screening of ten thousand-plus candidates through in-vitro testing to clinical trials; silicon design narrows from fast ISA simulators through RTL and logic synthesis to physical signoff. An isomorphic-filters arrow links the two columns, and a bottom bar notes that both funnels weed out high-scoring decoys before the expensive high-fidelity stages."}

Different tools therefore return different observations, and the environment cannot afford to blur them together. Physical-design tools make this staged feedback particularly clear. Logic synthesis, placement, routing, and signoff expose different observations and failure modes. The interface must state the stage, raw output, and tool-level status for each return. From logic synthesis through signoff, each stage returns its own observation class, failure modes, and an outcome to preserve (@tbl-eda-stage-interface).

::: {.callout-war-story title="Ariane 5 and the reused alignment module"}
**The claim.** Ariane 5 reused the inertial-reference alignment software from Ariane 4 for its maiden flight [@LionsAriane1996]. The code was flight-proven, so the team carried it over as already validated.

**The gap.** That module converted a 64-bit floating-point horizontal-velocity value into a 16-bit signed integer, a conversion that stayed in range only within Ariane 4's flight profile. Ariane 5 reached horizontal velocities roughly five times higher, the value overflowed, and the conversion raised an unhandled exception. The computation was dead code, needed only for Ariane 4's pre-launch alignment and useless once the vehicle had left the pad, yet it ran anyway and halted an otherwise-healthy inertial navigation system. The rocket self-destructed about 37 seconds after launch.

**The lesson.** The fault lived in the environment, not the intent. The alignment module ran to completion and returned a value; nothing in the flight objective was wrong. What failed was an assumption frozen into a reused component, a numeric range that no longer held once the surrounding vehicle changed. Architecture environments hide the same trap. A tool version, a reused wrapper's operating range, or the meaning of a return can go unrevalidated when the tool or the workload changes, and a run that exits cleanly then propagates a wrong result. The interface has to expose those assumptions so each study rechecks them against its own conditions rather than inheriting them on faith.
:::

| **EDA stage** | **Observation returned** | **Problem it can reveal** | **Tool-level outcome to preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Logic synthesis** | Mapped gates, area estimates, timing estimates, constraint warnings, and early power estimates. | Nonsynthesizable RTL, impossible constraints, and early area or timing problems. | A completed report, including declared constraint failures, is a valid observation; failure to produce the report is a tool-path failure. |
| **Floorplanning and placement** | Cell locations, utilization, congestion hints, timing pressure, and macro or memory placement effects. | Floorplans that create severe congestion, timing pressure, or integration problems. | Congestion or timing violations are valid observations from this stage, while an unsupported floorplan state remains out of scope. |
| **Clock, routing, and power closure** | Routed timing, clock behavior, congestion, design-rule checks, power integrity, and closure failures. | Physical effects absent from earlier tool stages. | Preserve each reported violation and warning separately from a timeout, license failure, or broken run. |
| **Signoff analysis** | Signoff reports, warning classes, violations tagged with the corner, mode, and library version they were measured under, and waived tool messages. | Conditions that remain unresolved at the end of the declared physical tool path. | Record the report and tool outcome without treating the tool status as an architecture decision. |

: **EDA stages return different findings.** From logic synthesis through signoff, each physical-design stage can reveal different candidate problems. To prevent AI hallucination, the environment must strictly map the output of the specific stage to the appropriate semantic meaning, never conflating an early synthesis estimate with a final signoff violation. {#tbl-eda-stage-interface tbl-colwidths="[20,25,25,30]"}

To balance determinism versus reproducibility, we must consider costs, operational fidelity, nondeterminism, and integrity. Two post-route attempts for the same hardware artifact may differ because of seed, thread count, host state, or tool heuristics. To manage nondeterminism and flakiness, distinguish three cases: expected statistical variation, declared tool nondeterminism, and flaky/unstable execution. Do not silently average contradictory returns from different stages, sources, or attempts.

Software engineering benchmarks like SWE-bench demonstrate that loosely connected scripts lead to unreproducible outcomes, so an agent needs explicit read, action, and return paths to avoid generating false positives. Architecture 2.0 must adopt the same discipline for tool execution, enforcing strict data provenance and reproducible environment snapshots. Much like modern cloud DevOps relies on immutable infrastructure, declaring a new state rather than manually patching a running server, architecture environments must enforce *immutable architecture states*.

The environment itself can bias the measurement. A classic systems result showed that changing nothing but the link order of a binary or the size of the UNIX environment shifts measured performance by more than the gain a typical optimization delivers [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. An optimizer given thousands of samples will find and exploit exactly such artifacts. Pinning tool versions, host state, and flags in the provenance record is therefore not bookkeeping but the control that keeps the agent learning the design's merits instead of the host's quirks.

Mutating a source file in place often corrupts the working directory when an EDA tool crashes. Rather than have the AI patch the broken directory with `sed`, early exploration actions branch from a pristine, immutable snapshot. However, always restarting from pristine RTL source is economically unviable in the deeper stages of the Silicon ADMET funnel, where physical design runs take days and generate gigabytes of intermediate databases. Thus, the environment must support incremental physical checkpoints, allowing the agent to branch from intermediate physical states (e.g., post-placement databases) for local optimization.

The fidelity pyramid of @sec-data-representations-world-models pairs cheap, abundant estimates with scarce ground truth, but the funnel filters correctly only if the cheap tier orders candidates the way the expensive tier would. That ordering is a measurable property rather than an article of faith. Before trusting an analytical model to screen a million candidates, promote a calibration batch through both tiers and compute the rank correlation between their scores. When the correlation decays, the cheap tier is manufacturing decoys instead of rejecting them. The correlation also sets the promotion count, because a weakly ranked tier must pass more survivors forward to keep the true winner in the pool.

## Beyond the Synchronous `env.step()` Loop

The standard machine learning loop assumes a synchronous `env.step()` function, where the agent takes a discrete action and the simulation instantly returns the new state and a reward. Because surviving the bottom of the Silicon ADMET funnel requires physical layout runs that take days to complete, this synchronous paradigm structurally fails. The Simulator Tax[^fn-simulator-tax-c06] shows up here in practice. An agent waiting for a synchronous `env.step()` could wait 8 hours for a physical routing failure in an EDA tool, compared to the 10 milliseconds it takes to receive a Python syntax error in a software environment. A physical synthesis flow cannot be driven through a blocking call, which will time out or hang when a placement job takes 40 hours or waits three days for an EDA license checkout.

[^fn-simulator-tax-c06]: **Simulator Tax**: The compute, wall-clock time, and license capacity an agent spends to obtain a single observation from an architecture tool, and the reason a design loop cannot answer uncertainty by simply taking more samples. The evaluation chapter later turns the tax into a measured quantity, scoring an agent on how much evidence it buys per unit of tool cost rather than on its final design alone.

Synchrony is only the most visible assumption this tutorial abstraction imports. Gym also assumes a cheap reset, yet an architecture environment has none; branching from a pristine snapshot is the closest equivalent, and every branch still pays real build and simulation cost. It assumes a Markov[^fn-markov-property-c06] step whose outcome depends only on the action, but EDA tools carry hidden cross-call state in caches, working directories, and license servers, which breaks the Markov assumption. It also expects a dense scalar reward after every step, whereas architectural feedback is sparse, arriving only at the end of a long chain of builds and checks, which leaves a poor final result hard to attribute to any single upstream action.

[^fn-markov-property-c06]: **Markov property**: The assumption that an environment's next state depends only on the current state and the chosen action, never on the longer history of how the system arrived there. Hidden cross-call state violates it, which is why stateless-looking tool wrappers mislead learning methods.

Each of these gaps has to be engineered away in the harness rather than the learning algorithm. The harness, not the agent that acts against it, is the deliverable.

Real tool chains require asynchronous, scarce, and protected execution mechanics. Long simulations, FPGA builds, EDA stages, and signoff require explicit submit, poll, resume, cancel, timeout, retry, queue, license, permission, artifact-isolation, and partial-return behavior. These are architecture environment semantics because they determine which candidate ran, which stage completed, which artifacts are valid, and whether another attempt is comparable.

Because returns arrive asynchronously and sometimes days late, omitting asynchronous state breaks the learning loop. From an ML-Sys perspective, the environment's "State" must dynamically include in-flight jobs and queue depth. If an agent dispatches 50 parallel multi-day EDA jobs and the environment hides this pending state, the agent's policy resubmits duplicate actions, spamming identical redundant work because it has no visibility into the queued jobs. Furthermore, the environment must stream intermediate surrogate rewards. The interface should emit partial observations as the job progresses (e.g., logic synthesis complete, initial timing estimates). This allows the RL agent to perform early trajectory pruning rather than waiting three days for a final binary routing failure.

In a commercial flow the binding resource is rarely a core. It is a license seat. A signoff-grade tool license is widely understood to cost on the order of an engineer's annual salary, and an installation owns only a handful, so the ceiling on parallel exploration is set by the license pool rather than the cluster. The harness must treat license tokens the way a scheduler treats GPUs, as admission-controlled capacity a job reserves before dispatch, and it must account for the human engineers sharing the same pool, because an agent that thrashes fifty checkouts starves the tapeout team down the hall.

A critical requirement of this asynchronous system is explicitly distinguishing between an infrastructure failure and an architectural constraint violation. If an agent proposes an SRAM configuration and the simulator crashes due to a host Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error, or because a license server went offline, this is an infrastructure failure. If the agent is penalized for this attempt, its policy will spuriously down-weight the SRAM configuration, polluting the design space exploration with infrastructure noise.

| **Failure type** | **Symptom** | **Environment action** | **Architectural meaning** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Infrastructure failure | Host out of memory, EDA license checkout timeout, cluster node crash. | Flag as `RETRY_ELIGIBLE` or `TOOL_CRASH`. | None. The candidate remains untested and must not be penalized in the design space. |
| Architectural constraint | Negative timing slack, unroutable netlist congestion, power-budget violation over 3 W. | Flag as valid evaluation return. | Negative design feedback. The candidate is physically infeasible and should be rejected or penalized. |

: **Cluster flakiness must never penalize a candidate:** When a host crash or license timeout aborts a run, the candidate remains untested and must not be down-weighted in the design space. The environment harness must trap infrastructure failures and handle them separately from true physical design constraints. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,30,25,25]"}

The environment harness must catch infrastructure failures and flag them appropriately (@tbl-failure-taxonomy), preventing the agent from optimizing against false negative signals. Only true architectural failures, such as failing to meet a timing constraint in synthesis or exceeding the system's 3 W power budget, should be passed back to the agent as negative design feedback.

Some tool crashes, however, carry real architectural signal. A pathological candidate can exhaust host memory, prove unroutable, or fail synthesis because its own resource footprint is infeasible rather than because the cluster is at fault. The harness cannot always separate the two before running, so it needs a retry-with-fingerprint rule. If the same candidate crashes the same tool in the same way across repeated attempts, the harness reclassifies the outcome from `TOOL_CRASH` to an architectural infeasibility signal.

However, merely returning a generic "failed" signal deprives the agent of architectural feedback. When a tool crashes (such as a router OOM due to an unroutable netlist), the environment wrapper should defensively parse *intermediate* or partial outputs, such as the last successful placement density map, to synthesize a negative architectural reward. By converting an uninformative infrastructure crash back into actionable design feedback, the agent parses the specific failure mode. To navigate this sparse architectural feedback, the environment must also formulate rewards as multi-objective Pareto-dominance signals (explicitly balancing Power, Performance, and Area) rather than a single scalar, enabling the agent to learn the physical trade-off frontier.

## The Three-Path Interface

A tool returns raw, unstructured text, but an architecture study needs structured observations it can compare, check, and store. Turning one into the other is the job of the environment interface.

Three words do distinct work in this chapter and are worth separating before they start appearing together. The environment is the whole connected surface a method acts against, covering every tool it may call and every observation it may receive. The wrapper is the layer around one tool that checks a request before it is issued, calls the tool, and parses what comes back. The harness is what records the run, its inputs, and its provenance so a later reader can tell what happened. One environment usually contains several wrappers and one harness.

![**The architecture environment interface.** An architecture environment connects a system intent to legal actions and translates raw tool outputs into semantic observations. The wrapper checks the request, calls the tool, and parses the result, while the harness records the run and its provenance.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="A diagram showing how an architecture environment connects an architecture question and workload, an action schema, and declared constraints and metric definitions to a wrapper and harness."}

An architecture environment explicitly maps intent to actions and actions to observations (@fig-environment-tool-interface). The wrapper acts as a protective boundary, intercepting high-level requests, validating them via the read path, executing tool commands via the action path, and distilling logs into a semantic vector via the return path.

### Defending Against Reward Hacking

The machine learning community has long warned of *reward hacking* [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete], a modern instance of Goodhart's Law, the observation that when a measure becomes an optimization target it stops being a good measure [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement]. Given a simple scalar reward, an optimizer may exploit the objective function to maximize that number while violating physical constraints [@OpenAIClark2016FaultyRewards]. In architecture, reward hacking manifests as physically impossible designs. If an environment merely reports IPC without constraints, the optimizer might propose a 10-terabyte L1 cache or a 100-port SRAM to maximize the score. Either structure looks brilliant in functional simulation, posting an IPC no real machine reaches, and is rejected on sight by physical synthesis for routing congestion and area the functional model never represented. Nothing bounded the proxy by the physics, so the optimizer was free to leave the physics behind, which is what the downstream constraints of the Silicon ADMET funnel exist to prevent.

Because physical design limits dictate architectural choices bottom-up, ground truth from traditional EDA tools is the environment's first defense against these AI exploits, indispensable for enforcing laws like timing closure and power limits. The full defense discipline, converting tool feedback into evidence that can reject a candidate, is @sec-feedback-verification-trust's subject; the environment's job is to keep the physical constraints in the loop at all.

### Formalizing the Paths

To make this data usable, the environment establishes three distinct paths:

1. **The Read Path:** This supplies state references, fixed context, permissions, and economic budgets *before* an action is proposed. Cluster hours are the obvious budget and usually not the binding one. Where a tool license pool limits parallel exploration, the read path has to expose seat availability too, because an agent shown only core-hours will plan an escalation the license queue will not admit. This allows the agent to balance the fidelity of its proposed action against the cost of execution. The environment must explicitly contrast the trivial compute cost of model inference against the much larger economic cost of the target EDA simulation.
2. **The Action Path:** To prevent unsafe or nonsensical proposals, the Action Path exposes a *safe-by-construction* action space. However, architectural parameters are rarely independent (e.g., cache capacity, block size, and associativity dictate if the number of sets is valid; memory timings have strict inter-dependencies). The environment wrapper must act as a **constraint solver**, intercepting algebraically invalid combinations *before* invoking the simulator. Projecting the agent's independent mutations onto a strictly legal hardware manifold prevents physically impossible states from ever reaching the tool.
3. **The Return Path:** This carries typed tool returns, raw artifacts, cost, latency, provenance, and terminal outcomes. A single typed return is rarely one number. An architecture observation vector carries the performance and physical signals the downstream method compares, among them IPC and cache miss rates from the simulator, functional-unit and interconnect utilization, a power estimate, worst-case timing slack, design-rule check violation counts from the physical flow, and log-derived error classes for warnings the parser recognized but could not score. The scalar reward a method optimizes is a projection of this vector, not the vector itself, which is why the interface stores every component with its provenance rather than collapsing them early. Those three terms are the atoms of a valid measurement. A *corner* is a named combination of process, voltage, and temperature the tools analyze at; a *mode* is an operating configuration such as functional, test, or a low-power state; and the *library version* fixes which characterized standard cells the numbers came from. A slack number without its corner is not an observation. Minus twelve picoseconds at the slow corner, low voltage, high temperature is a different fact from minus twelve picoseconds at the typical corner, and signoff evaluates every mode and corner combination separately. The return path's schema must carry the corner, mode, and library version alongside every timing and power figure, or two runs that look identical in the record are not the same measurement. Why multi-corner closure exists is @sec-feedback-verification-trust's territory; the narrower requirement here is that the observation type preserve it. To manage micro-architectural nondeterminism (like OS thread scheduling or asynchronous I/O noise in full-system simulators), the environment must orchestrate multiple statistical samples. Instead of returning a single noisy scalar IPC, the environment should return a *confidence interval*, forcing the AI to optimize for robust architectural gains rather than exploiting statistical artifacts.

An agent's action space can range from simple parameter tuning to complex structural mutations (like rewriting an MLIR dataflow graph). By encapsulating these within a formalized read/action cycle, the environment protects the physical infrastructure from rogue agent behaviors.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Rather than providing raw Python code, we can also formalize the overall execution loop as a standard algorithmic interface (@lst-environment-interface), drawing inspiration from frameworks like OpenAI Gym and its Farama-maintained successor Gymnasium, but tailored for the unique constraints of hardware design [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium].
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
Rather than providing raw Python code, we can also formalize the overall execution loop as a standard algorithmic interface (Algorithm~\ref{lst-environment-interface}), drawing inspiration from frameworks like OpenAI Gym and its Farama-maintained successor Gymnasium, but tailored for the unique constraints of hardware design [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium].
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\begin{algorithm}[H]
\caption{\textbf{One validated action becomes one recorded run:} the interface rejects illegal actions before touching a tool, submits work asynchronously, separates infrastructure crashes from architectural failures, and returns a typed observation with provenance.}\label{lst-environment-interface}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require \texttt{action\_request} (e.g., target L2 cache size, routing effort)
\Ensure \texttt{observation\_vector}, \texttt{status\_flags}, \texttt{provenance\_metadata}
\State \textbf{Validate Action (Read/Action Path):}
\If{\texttt{action\_request} violates fixed constraints}
    \State \Return \texttt{INVALID\_ACTION} immediately. Do not invoke tools.
\EndIf
\State \textbf{Translate to Tool Commands:}
\State Lower \texttt{action\_request} into tool-specific configurations.
\State \textbf{Asynchronous Execution (Return Path):}
\State \texttt{job\_id} $\gets$ \text{Submit job to cluster/queue.}
\State \Return \texttt{PENDING(job\_id)} immediately.
\State \dots \textit{Later, upon polling \texttt{job\_id}:} \dots
\If{infrastructure fails (timeout, missing license)}
    \State \Return \texttt{TOOL\_CRASH}. Do not penalize the architecture candidate.
\EndIf
\State \textbf{Data Distillation:}
\State Parse the tool stdout and trace files.
\State Extract KPIs into \texttt{observation\_vector}.
\State \textbf{Return State:}
\State Package \texttt{observation\_vector}, \texttt{status\_flags}, and exact tool hashes.
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {#lst-environment-interface .algorithm lst-cap="**One validated action becomes one recorded run:** the interface rejects illegal actions before touching a tool, submits work asynchronously, separates infrastructure crashes from architectural failures, and returns a typed observation with provenance."}
**Require:** `action_request`
**Ensure:** `observation_vector`, `status_flags`, `provenance_metadata`

1. **Validate Action (Read/Action Path):**

   - If `action_request` violates fixed constraints:
     - **return** `INVALID_ACTION` immediately. Do not invoke tools.
2. **Translate to Tool Commands:**

   - Lower `action_request` into tool-specific configurations (e.g., CACTI `.cfg`).
3. **Asynchronous Execution (Return Path):**

   - Submit job to cluster/queue and obtain `job_id`.
   - **return** `PENDING(job_id)` immediately.
   - *... Later, the caller resumes by polling `job_id`, which returns `PENDING` until the job terminates and then yields the same observation vector a synchronous call would have produced. The `job_id` is the study's handle on that result, so it is recorded with the candidate at submission time rather than at completion, and a result whose handle was never recorded cannot be attached to the candidate that requested it ...*
   - If infrastructure fails:
     - **return** `TOOL_CRASH`. Do not penalize candidate.
4. **Data Distillation:**

   - Parse tool stdout and trace files.
   - Extract KPIs into `observation_vector`.
5. **Return State:**

   - Package `observation_vector`, `status_flags`, and exact tool hashes.
:::
:::

Distinct read, action, and return paths let an architecture environment carry architectural intent across domain boundaries, from the compiler's intermediate representation to the final physical design signoff. The environment stops short of making the architectural decision, which keeps it a trusted observation platform.

If another method can act in the same harness and another architect can interpret its results without private knowledge, the environment is sound. Generative models and optimization algorithms can then operate on the environment independently.

That test is only worth stating if a real environment can be written down against it. The study in @sec-running-the-loop ran inside a small one, and its contract fits in a table (@tbl-environment-contract). Nothing in it is elaborate. What makes it an environment rather than a script is that every row was fixed before a candidate was measured, and that the last row exists at all.

| **Contract field** | **The array-study harness** |
| --- | --- |
| **Fixed context** | SCALE-Sim at a pinned version, weight-stationary dataflow, and frozen SRAM capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, and workload matrices. |
| **Legal actions** | Set the array height and width to one of fifteen declared shapes. Nothing else is mutable, so the search cannot widen its own space. |
| **What the tool returns** | Cycle counts, per-layer utilization, and memory traffic, computed from an analytical dataflow model. |
| **What the tool cannot tell you** | Nothing about timing closure, power, or physical design. The environment is silent on those axes rather than optimistic about them, and a claim on any of them needs a different tool. |
| **Invalid-state behavior** | A candidate outside the declared shape set is refused before the simulator is invoked. A malformed model response triggers one repair call. Either way the attempt is recorded. |
| **Cost of an observation** | An equal, predeclared simulator-call budget for both arms, so neither can buy its result with extra evaluations. |
| **Repeatability** | Deterministic under the frozen configuration. Retained inputs and hashes let another architect rerun the same computation, which is replay and not independent validation. |
| **What the environment may not decide** | Whether the workload is representative, whether the score is the right objective, or whether a result authorizes RTL work. The harness ranks candidates and owns none of those. |

: **An environment contract is short, and the last row is the one that makes it an environment:** each field was fixed before any candidate was measured, and the harness ranks candidates without acquiring authority over what its ranking means. {#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

Write this table before the first tool call, not after the last one. Filled afterward it is a description, and a description cannot refuse anything.

The Return Path is where a raw tool log becomes the observation the agent acts on. But capturing the return safely is only the first step; we must also ensure the AI can parse it.

## Attention Bottlenecks and Distillation

When interfacing models with traditional architecture tools, a mismatch occurs at the observation layer. A commercial EDA tool or a detailed simulator like gem5 generates exhaustive text output, often containing tens of thousands of lines. If an environment wrapper naively pipes raw stdout directly back to the agent, the relevant signals stay buried in the noise, making it harder to debug the actual hardware issue.

A critical requirement of the Return Path is **Data Distillation**. Because traditional architecture and EDA tools are verbose, the architect must build robust *log-to-semantic parsers* into the environment wrapper.

This creates an asymmetry. We can bound the agent's *input* actions using compiler IRs like CIRCT, but the *output* from legacy EDA tools remains an unstructured stream of text. While modern tools offer clean Python APIs (like OpenROAD), legacy commercial flows rely on Tcl. Crucially, Tcl shells (like `dc_shell`[^fn-dc-shell-c06]) are stateful, side-effect-heavy REPLs, not clean APIs. The environment wrapper must therefore inject self-trapping scripts (e.g., using `catch`) that serialize their own structured JSON, shielding the agent from Tcl's fragility.

[^fn-dc-shell-c06]: **dc_shell**: The interactive command shell of a commercial logic synthesis tool, driven by Tcl scripts. Like any read-eval-print loop it accumulates state across commands, so what a command returns depends on every command issued before it, which is the opposite of the stateless request an API contract assumes.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The swallowed synthesis warning"}
**The trap.** A continuous integration (CI) script or parsing regex was tuned to known synthesis errors to catch design-rule violations.

**The mechanism.** The script silently swallowed a new, unclassified warning about a downgraded timing constraint and a miswired clock domain crossing buried deep in the log text. Because the regex only flagged what it knew, the warning never reached a human, and the defect it described survived into silicon.

**The lesson.** Log parsers cannot afford to discard the unknown. This grounds the need to preserve "unclassified anomalies" alongside structured JSON, ensuring that critical but unfamiliar warnings are not filtered away from the agent's attention. This case is a composite of a recurring log-parsing failure pattern, not one documented incident.
:::

Much like DevOps engineers use monitoring tools to distill millions of server logs into key metrics, architecture environments must translate sprawling outputs into structured summaries. Consider our Lighthouse XR prompt: if the vector accelerator exceeds its power budget, returning the raw 5,000-line power analysis log will immediately hit the LLM's "telemetry wall" and exhaust its context window. The environment wrapper must parse the EDA log, filter out irrelevant setup warnings, and distill the violation into a clean JSON observation (e.g., `{"violation": "power_budget", "peak_w": 3.4, "budget_w": 3.0}`). Furthermore, for unclassified anomalies that cannot be mapped to a simple schema, the parser must apply mechanical truncation and semantic filtering (e.g., extracting the last 50 lines before a FATAL tag). This preserves the actionable failure string without overflowing the context window.

Distillation must preserve, not discard, unclassified anomalies. A parser tuned to known design-rule violations can silently drop the swapped library corner, downgraded constraint, or version-deprecation notice that a brownfield debug actually turns on. A safer wrapper returns two channels, a structured vector of the recognized metrics and violations alongside a flagged residual of the unparsed warning and error lines plus an integrity hash of the full log, so the agent gets a dense observation without the harness deciding on its own that a warning was irrelevant.

Representing a tool like Yosys or OpenROAD for an agent involves defining its input schema (e.g., accepted flags, valid file formats, constraint objects), its execution bounds, and its structured outputs (e.g., JSON-formatted area and timing reports rather than raw text stdout). However, agents eventually hit a telemetry wall, because context windows restrict how much output they can observe. When an API serializes a large physical layout into text, it risks lossy serialization.

Truncating a million-line timing trace to fit a context window creates a permanent verification blind spot for the AI, causing it to falsely predict success because the error was paginated away. Formalizing tools as typed APIs with explicit failure modes and hierarchical summarization lets the agent programmatically construct valid toolchain requests. It parses the resulting metrics directly into its internal state, executing deterministic recovery actions without hitting the telemetry wall. The architect ultimately reviews these structured summaries in the evaluation harness to ensure thermal budgets and STA hold.

## Hardware API Standardization

While a robust three-path interface manages execution, the payloads traversing those paths must be mathematically and structurally unambiguous. Historically, hardware descriptions relied on languages such as SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800) built for human designers and proprietary logic synthesizers, not programmatic mutation. The fragmentation is real, but it lives in the subset of the standard each tool supports and in vendor Tcl and constraint dialects, not in the language's ownership.

If an agent relies on text-based string-matching or shallow Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) parsing to modify a Verilog module, it will corrupt the design. Textual regex cannot safely resolve tangled macro expansions, evaluate parameterized `generate` blocks, or infer the unspoken module hierarchies that ultimately dictate physical placement and routing.

This brittleness necessitates the *Standardization of Hardware APIs* through open, formally structured intermediary representations, most notably MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation) and its hardware-centric counterpart CIRCT (Circuit IR Compilers and Tools).

CIRCT replaces unstructured text with a strict, queryable Static Single Assignment (SSA)[^fn-ssa-c06] form that explicitly models dataflow, concurrency, and structural dependencies.

[^fn-ssa-c06]: **Static Single Assignment (SSA)**: A compiler intermediate form in which every value is defined exactly once and never reassigned, so a program's dataflow is explicit in its structure. For hardware, this is what makes an IR graph traversable and checkable in a way raw Verilog text is not. CIRCT captures hardware intent as a graph of progressive dialects, stepping down from high-level abstractions (`firrtl` or `handshake`) to structural nets (`hw` and `comb`), which gives AI agents a typed, deterministic interface.

Instead of blind text mutation, an agent can programmatically walk the SSA graph to inject a pipeline register or re-balance a datapath, relying on the compiler framework to enforce semantic legality by construction.

For the human architect, these standardized representations form an indispensable safety boundary. They ensure the AI's intent survives translation across the physical toolchain, and they rule out structurally illegal states by construction. Physical realizability is a separate question, and it still comes from the downstream tools that measure timing, power, and congestion.

## Orchestrating Complex Toolchains

When a candidate design successfully navigates the Three-Path Interface and its intent is safely encoded in a standardized IR like MLIR, it must be translated into actionable physical tool commands. However, a single high-level intent rarely maps to a single tool. A hardware configuration might need to fan out to multiple distinct evaluation backends. These include an RTL simulator for functional correctness, a VLSI flow for power and area estimates, and an FPGA emulation path for full-stack software booting.

![**The Chipyard framework.** Chipyard, an open-source RISC-V SoC generator, routes a single configuration downward to three backend evaluation paths: RTL simulation, VLSI flow, and FPGA emulation. This fan-out ensures one configuration reaches every evaluation path consistently.](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A flow diagram of the Chipyard SoC-generation framework. A configuration system feeds Chisel generators (Rocket, BOOM, Hwacha) into the FIRRTL compiler, which fans the single configuration out to three backend paths: RTL simulation, a VLSI flow, and FPGA emulation."}

The environment framework routes one candidate architecture change downward into several legal tool actions without losing its connection to the system intent (@fig-chipyard-framework).

### Declarative Execution Planning

To manage this fan-out, we must look to adjacent domains that have solved this exact problem of decoupling *intent* from *messy execution mechanics*.

In Database Query Optimization, a software engineer declares *what* data they want via a SQL query, never specifying *how* to read the disk or which B-tree to traverse. A query planner analyzes the request, checks its cached data, evaluates the compute budget, and builds an optimal execution plan dynamically. Similarly, an architecture environment can act as a query planner for evaluations. Instead of the AI imperatively calling a specific simulator script, it should issue a declarative hypothesis: `Evaluate(Candidate=Lighthouse_V2, Metric=IPC)`. The environment then determines whether to serve a cached result, query a fast analytical model, or provision a 24-hour RTL simulation based on the current budget constraints.

In computational biology, executing a genomic pipeline previously required brittle bash scripts. Frameworks like Nextflow [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow] and Snakemake [@KosterEtAl2012Snakemake] emerged to formalize dataflow, isolating the *scientific logic* from the *execution mechanics* (cluster queues, retries, and tool crashes). In cloud computing, Kubernetes relies on desired-state reconciliation. The user declares the intent, and the orchestration engine handles the low-level failures. These frameworks abstract execution mechanics into a formal graph, letting the architect review high-level declarative goals instead of debugging why a synthesis job crashed on node 4.

Architecture 2.0 environments must act as this orchestration layer. A semantic proposal may require several reads, transformations, builds, executions, and checks. Their dependencies form a graph rather than a single call or mandatory sequence.

Fulfilling the Lighthouse prompt for a complex System-on-Chip (SoC) means orchestrating the design intent through the Chipyard generator framework as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies. Integrating the low-power RISC-V compute subsystem with custom XR accelerators requires explicit lowering from MLIR to RTL, along with related compiler IR transformations. The dataflow moves through several precise stages. An agent's high-level intent first triggers an MLIR lowering to emit new spatial-tracking instructions, which then informs a hardware target feature declaration within the Chipyard configuration.

That configuration fans out into multiple execution branches. It generates RTL, which in turn feeds both a rebuilt custom Linux binary for a functional correctness run in Verilator, an open-source RTL simulator, and a physical logic synthesis flow that checks routing congestion and verifies the power budget. The environment acts as the arbiter of this DAG, running some branches in parallel while others block until earlier artifacts exist, so the AI's edits are vetted against physical realities before they are presented back for review.

One branch is missing from this fan-out, and in real projects it is the largest. The Wilson study cited earlier puts more than half of project effort into verifying that a design still computes the right answers, and an AI-mutated RTL block raises that burden rather than lowering it. The orchestrator must place the correctness checks (lint, equivalence checking, and regression suites) as the first and cheapest stages of the DAG, short-circuiting synthesis and layout when a candidate fails them, because an IPC number measured on functionally wrong RTL is not evidence of anything. The machinery of those checks belongs to @sec-feedback-verification-trust; their position at the front of the execution graph belongs here.

### Sandbox Resilience

EDA tools and cycle-level simulators are notoriously brittle, slow, and expensive to run. A generated RTL block can spin in an infinite elaboration loop, a router can segfault on a pathological netlist, and a synthesis script can wedge a license daemon. The architecture environment must act as a resilient sandbox so one bad candidate does not take down the host or corrupt a shared working tree. Process isolation keeps each tool invocation in its own address space and filesystem view, resource caps bound its memory and disk footprint, and a wall-clock timeout on every stage catches the elaboration that never terminates. When a tool panics or raises a segmentation fault, the harness traps the signal, records the partial outputs and exit status, and returns control to the loop rather than letting the failure unwind the whole study. This resilience is a systems property, distinct from safe exploration in the reinforcement-learning sense, which constrains which actions an agent may take while it is still learning.

### Artifact Lineage and Provenance

To illustrate this orchestration complexity, consider how a single architecture proposal formally splits into specific software and hardware instantiations (@fig-artifact-lineage).

![**Artifact lineage and cryptographic provenance.** A single Lighthouse intent fans out into software binaries and hardware RTL, each hashed to ensure reproducible evaluations.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="Artifact Lineage and Cryptographic Provenance. A single Lighthouse intent fans out into software binaries and hardware RTL, each hashed to ensure reproducible evaluations."}

Software variant S2 may be an MLIR-derived lowering compiled into binary B2. Hardware variant H3 may be a Chipyard-derived configuration elaborated into RTL R3. Changing B2 while holding R3 fixed creates a new evaluation instance even if the root proposal is unchanged.

An evaluation instance binds every layer relevant to that tool action. Each transformation records parent, tool and transformation version, input identifiers, output identifiers, content hashes where useful, and the intended semantic relation. A semantics-changing edit creates a child candidate. Google's Bazel [@Bazel] build system guarantees reproducibility by enforcing hermeticity, where every output is addressed by a cryptographic hash of its inputs. This matches the architectural need to track hardware candidate identity as it lowers from a C++ memory model to RTL to Layout. A hash proves artifact identity, not architectural or functional equivalence.

## Open Research Questions

An environment is a research object in its own right rather than a wrapper around whichever tools a project happens to own. What stays open is how far a cheap tier can be trusted to screen for an expensive one, what a return means when the tool carries state between calls, and what a simulation can establish about silicon.

**Theme 1: Screening Cascades and Promotion.** A cheap fidelity tier earns its place only if it orders candidates the way the expensive tier would, and how well it does that is measurable rather than a matter of faith.

- How many candidates must a cheap tier promote to keep the true best design in the pool, given its measured rank correlation with the expensive tier?
- What share of an evaluation budget should be spent measuring the correlation between two tiers rather than screening candidates with them?
- What signal reveals that a cheap tier has begun manufacturing decoys, before an expensive tier is spent discovering it?

**Theme 2: Learning Against a Stateful Environment.** Architecture tools hold state across calls, return days late and out of order, and sometimes fail for reasons that belong to the cluster rather than to the candidate.

- How can a harness decide whether a crash reflects a broken environment or a candidate whose own resource footprint is infeasible?
- When does a design change invalidate evidence collected under the previous design, such as a trace whose speculative paths no longer exist?
- How should a search assign credit when observations arrive days later, out of order, and preceded by partial results?

**Theme 3: The Constraints That Actually Bind.** Equivalence checking and regression on AI-mutated RTL is the largest verification branch in real projects, and tool license seats rather than compute cores set the true ceiling on parallel exploration. Neither has an answer here.

- What equivalence and regression strategy keeps pace with a generator that mutates RTL faster than a full regression can run, and what may be safely skipped between full runs?
- How should an environment schedule against a license pool, and what does an agent need to see about seat availability in order to reason about whether an expensive tier is affordable at all?

**Theme 4: Bridging the Sim-to-Silicon Gap.** A design can pass every simulation and still fail in silicon, and the dimensions a simulator cannot see are exactly the ones an optimizer is free to exploit.

- Which measurement conditions must an observation carry for a candidate ranking to survive a change of corner, mode, or library version?
- How can an environment detect that an agent is exploiting a physical dimension its current fidelity cannot verify?
- What models can trace a late-stage signoff violation back to the upstream mutation that caused it?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="The Action Space Must Not Exceed Oracle Fidelity"}
Never allow an agent to propose architectural changes that the available simulator or formal tool cannot verify. If an agent mutates a thermal property but the EDA loop only runs logic simulation, it will silently exploit the unchecked dimension. The permitted action space should not reach past the physical dimensions some check in the budget can observe, and where it must, the unobserved dimension is declared rather than left for the optimizer to find.
:::


An architecture environment transforms opaque tool executions into an explicit interface that automated methods and human architects can trust. It records precisely which tensor-enabled software artifact ran against which hardware artifact, exactly which tools completed, which actions failed or lacked support, and the typed meaning of every return.

A well-maintained environment is the contract that makes AI-driven architectural discovery reproducible and auditable, and that routes every candidate to the tools which decide whether it is physically valid. The environment does not confer validity. It guarantees that the question reached an instrument able to answer it, and that the answer came back with enough provenance to be trusted, which is where @sec-feedback-verification-trust begins.

::: {.callout-carry-forward}
- **Carry forward:** An architecture environment exposes a read, action, and return interface so a candidate change reaches legal tool actions and every raw tool output becomes a typed observation another architect can inspect. That typed return must say whether the tool failed or the candidate did, and it must keep the warnings no parser could classify. It also carries a price and an error bar, because a tier of the fidelity spectrum is a purchase rather than a lookup, and it belongs to a hashed software-and-hardware evaluation instance, so two numbers are comparable only when they name the same instance.
- **Reader test:** Can another method act in the same harness, and can another architect read one of your timing numbers and name the corner, mode, and library version behind it, without private knowledge from whoever built the environment?
- **Up next:** The loop can now represent state, propose changes, and execute them against real tools. But when the environment returns an observation (a passing DRC, a failed synthesis run, a timing report), how do we know we can trust it? In @sec-feedback-verification-trust, we take up the foundation of the Evaluate stage, where raw observations become rigorous feedback, verified claims, and architectural trust.
:::
